one_liner: Apache Fory's C++ serializer for plain annotated structs, cross-language binary format; 1.3-11x Protobuf's throughput in its benchmarks.
what_it_does: Serializes ordinary C++ structs and classes (std::string, vector, map, optional, variant, smart pointers) that you annotate with a FORY_STRUCT(...) field-list macro and register by numeric ID or name. No generated message classes are needed, although the foryc compiler can generate native structs from Fory IDL or existing .proto files. The API is a builder-configured Fory object with serialize / serialize_to(Buffer&) / deserialize<T> that return Result<T, Error> instead of throwing. The default xlang mode writes bytes that the Java, Python, Go, Rust, JS, C# and other Fory implementations can read; .xlang(false) selects a C++-only native mode, and a separate row format gives zero-copy random field access.
how_it_is_fast: FORY_STRUCT generates constexpr field metadata, and fields are sorted at compile time: non-nullable fixed-width primitives come first by size, then varints, then everything else. The serializer can therefore reserve the maximum size once and write the leading primitives at compile-time offsets with a single writer-index update, skipping per-field capacity checks and error propagation. It encodes straight from the user's struct with no intermediate message object, using zigzag varints for int32/int64 and a combined length-plus-encoding header for strings (Latin-1/UTF-16/UTF-8). In compatible mode, schema metadata (a TypeDef identified by a 52-bit MurmurHash3 hash) is written once per stream and cached by the reader, and per-field reads are unrolled through compile-time switch dispatch.
when_to_use: C++ code that already models data as plain structs (strings, vectors, maps, nested structs) and today pays to copy them into protobuf message objects and back; that conversion is where the benchmark's biggest serialize wins (4-11x) come from
Throughput-bound serialization of small-to-medium messages (roughly 80 B to 2 KB in the benchmarks), using one Fory instance per thread and a reused Buffer via serialize_to
Payloads exchanged between C++ and Java/Python/Go/Rust/JS/C# services that should share one wire format, with type IDs registered consistently or types generated from Fory/protobuf IDL
Object graphs with shared or cyclic std::shared_ptr references (track_ref(true)), which protobuf cannot express
Rolling deployments that need add/remove/reorder field evolution (compatible mode is the default); for C++-only, same-schema traffic, .xlang(false).compatible(false) gives smaller, faster payloads
when_not_to_use: You need protobuf wire compatibility, preservation of unknown fields, or protobuf/gRPC tooling (reflection, interceptors). Fory bytes are not protobuf bytes, and its own docs recommend protobuf for these cases

Payload size matters more than CPU. In the 2026-06-12 report Fory's output was larger than Protobuf's for Sample (445 vs 375 B) and MediaContent (362 vs 301 B); it was smaller only for the numeric structs
Large messages where you read a few fields in place. Object mode decodes the whole struct; flat formats (or Fory's separate row format) avoid that

You need a long-stable C++ API. The C++ object-graph serializer arrived in November 2025, and v1.7.0 through v1.7.5 shipped within four weeks (2026-08-28 to 2026-09-25), alongside codec-boundary hardening commits in late August 2026

Decoding untrusted input without extra setup. The C++ security guide requires registering only accepted types and keeping the graph-memory and depth limits; Fory's Java and Python implementations have had deserialization CVEs (CVE-2025-59328, CVE-2026-50076, CVE-2025-61622, CVE-2026-48207), and none are listed for C++

integration.form: static lib (or shared); a compiled library pulled in with CMake FetchContent (SOURCE_SUBDIR cpp, target fory::serialization) or as a Bazel module; not header-only
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (MurmurHash3 and its hash map are vendored); googletest only for tests; gRPC C++ 1.39+ only for the generated gRPC companions; the foryc compiler is optional, for IDL codegen
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; CMake 3.16+ or Bazel 8+. The docs disagree on compiler minimums: the install guide lists GCC 7+/Clang 5+/MSVC 2017+, the benchmark README GCC 8+/Clang 7+/MSVC 2019+. MSVC requires /Zc:preprocessor
integration.platforms: x86-64 (CMake compiles Fory's sources with -mavx2 or /arch:AVX2 by default), aarch64 (NEON paths), plus SSE2 and scalar fallbacks; CI runs on ubuntu-latest, macos-latest and windows-2022, with ASan/UBSan jobs
integration.thread_safety: A Fory instance is not thread-safe (it is the fastest option; use one per thread). build_thread_safe() returns a ThreadSafeFory backed by a pool of instances. Register types before starting threads.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: foryc can compile existing .proto schemas into plain C++ structs with Fory serializers, but the wire format is not protobuf-compatible, unknown fields are not preserved, and the API (FORY_STRUCT + register_struct + Result<T, Error>) differs from generated protobuf classes

gotchas: Each struct needs a FORY_STRUCT(...) list placed after its fields (in a public: section inside a class), plus register_struct<T>(id) on every Fory instance. A missing registration fails at runtime with 'Type not registered', not at compile time.
The defaults are track_ref(true) and compatible(true), and both cost speed and size. The published benchmark switched reference tracking off, so disable it for value-shaped data.
On x86-64, CMake's FORY_USE_AVX2 option defaults to ON and adds -mavx2 to Fory's compiled sources. Set it to OFF if the binary must run on CPUs without AVX2.

With compatible(false), mismatched schemas 'may cause errors or undefined behavior' (per the docs). Even in compatible mode, renaming a field is not supported because fields match by snake_case name or tag ID. Raw pointers and std::array are listed as unsupported.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Fory over YaFF, SBE or ProtoCache when you want to decode into ordinary owning C++ structs (strings, vectors, maps, shared_ptr graphs) with schema evolution on by default and readers in other languages. Pick SBE for fixed-layout, low-latency messages, and YaFF or ProtoCache when you read a few fields in place from a buffer without a full decode.
verified_claims_summary: Fory's own Google Benchmark suite (xlang compatible mode, reference tracking off, reused output buffer) against Protobuf v25.5, built Release with -O3 on an unnamed compiler, ran on a 12-core, 48 GB arm64 Mac (Darwin 24.6.0, chip not named). Its 2026-06-12 report shows 1.27x-10.9x Protobuf's throughput, e.g. MediaContent serialize at 8.81M vs 2.12M ops/s (4.15x). Most of the Protobuf timings include converting to and from plain C++ structs on every iteration; on Sample, the one case that uses native protobuf objects, Fory was 1.59x on serialize and 2.25x on deserialize. The older benchmarks/cpp README table (Darwin 24.5.0) shows 1.2x-4.5x.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-23, v1.7.5 released 2026-09-25) and Apache-2.0 licensed, but the C++ object serializer is under a year old and is consumed as a CMake or Bazel-built library rather than vendored headers.
